newsitem.title: UK: U.S. payrolls cast shadow over bonds rally.
newsitem.headline: U.S. payrolls cast shadow over bonds rally.

text.p: Global bonds, basking in the strength of the current rally, could be brought down to earth after the U.S. figures for people in employment during in November due out on Friday, analysts said.
A figure above forecasts could add to existing concerns that the rally has gone too far, and trigger a decline in U.S. government bonds which could feed through into other markets, they said.
"The big problem is that the U.S. rally is starting to look tired and has been struggling for the last couple of days," said Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International in London.
"The payrolls report has got to be one factor which could cause bond investors to rethink their positions."
A Reuters poll forecast the November U.S. payrolls report to show a rise of 179,000, compared with a rise of 210,000 in October. The unemployment rate is expected to be stable at 5.2 percent.
Hannah said his own forecast of a rise of 220,000 was at the upper end of expectations, and would be likely to "take the froth off the bond markets."
Lee Ferridge, Treasury economist at NatWest Capital Markets in London, said the U.S. long bond was not attractive with a yield of around 6.37 percent.
"The balance of risks is for a shakeout in the next couple of days," Ferridge said.
He said an average earnings rise of 0.4 percent, currently the consensus forecast, would be sufficient to give the market a shock.
However, Andy Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London said sentiment was so buoyant that it would be difficult for even a strong number to turn it around.

"Clearly the thing that has motivated the rally is the belief that there are no underlying inflationary pressures that will drive the Fed (Federal Reserve) to have to think in terms of tightening," said Bevan.
"The market has been shifting closer to the view that there could even be some chance for an ease in the early part of the year," he said, adding a cut in rates was unlikely.

Although he said economic data were likely to show a pick up in the fourth quarter, they were not expected to be significant enough to stoke fears that the Fed will raise interest rates in the first quarter.
However, Bevan expected the rally to begin petering out in 1997.
With yields in major bond markets already low, some analysts were questioning whether there was any scope for further gains, particularly for European bonds.
"There is nothing ahead on the European horizon, in terms of good news, that has not already been anticipated," said Hannah.
Bevan said recent talk of France putting pressure on the Bundesbank to ease interest rates was overdone, and had contributed to an over-extension of the rally in German and French government bonds.
He said the risk was that 10-year Bund yields could correct back to 5.85-5.90 percent from 5.66 percent currently.
Hannah advised looking at dollar bloc bond markets, such as Canada or Australia as alternatives, while cash also offered better potential than many bond markets.
Phyllis Reed, bond strategist at BZW in London said it was getting harder and harder to find value in bonds.
"Cash offers a good alternative in the U.S., although it's not so good in core Europe," she said. "I'd be looking at holding dollars until the Treasury bond market backs up a bit."
